structure.title: I.
structure.summary: On a cold, wet night at Laburnam Villa, Mr. and Mrs. White and their son Herbert are playing chess by a fireside when Sergeant-Major Morris, an old friend returning from India, arrives by foot after a long journey. Over whiskey, Morris recounts tales of distant lands and reveals the existence of a monkey’s paw, a dried talisman enchanted by a fakir to grant three wishes to three different men, but with dire consequences — the previous owner wished for death as his third wish. Despite Morris’s warnings and his attempt to burn the paw, Mr. White retrieves it, and after being goaded by Herbert, he makes a careless wish for two hundred pounds. The paw twists in his hand as he speaks, and though no money appears immediately, the family is left unsettled by the eerie movement and the oppressive silence that follows.

structure.title: II.
characters_present: the stranger from Maw and Meggins
structure.summary: The chapter opens on a bright wintry morning at the White family home, where the parents and their son Herbert laugh off the supernatural claims of the monkey's paw, dismissing it as the delusion of an old soldier. The paw is carelessly tossed on the sideboard, and the family enjoys a lighthearted breakfast, with Herbert teasing his father about greed before leaving for work on foot. Later, during dinner, Mr. White insists the paw moved in his hand, while Mrs. White grows uneasy as a well-dressed stranger in a glossy silk hat hesitates outside their gate before entering. The man, sent by the firm 'Maw and Meggins,' delivers the devastating news that Herbert has been killed in a machinery accident at work, and that the company offers two hundred pounds as compensation — the exact amount wished for earlier. Overcome by the horrifying coincidence, Mr. White collapses unconscious as his wife lets out a shriek.

structure.title: III.
structure.summary: In the aftermath of their son Herbert's death, an elderly couple retreats into silent grief in their shadowed house, two miles from the cemetery where he was buried. A week later, the wife, consumed by desperate hope, demands her husband retrieve the monkey’s paw — a supernatural talisman that granted one wish already — and use it to bring their son back to life. Though horrified and terrified by the prospect of confronting his mutilated corpse, the husband reluctantly wishes for Herbert's return. As they wait in dread, a stealthy knock sounds at the front door, escalating into violent pounding; the wife rushes to open it, while the husband frantically searches the floor for the paw to undo the wish. He finds it just as the final bolt is drawn and breathes his third wish, after which the knocking ceases and the house is left in chilling silence.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
On a cold, wet night at Laburnam Villa, Mr. and Mrs. White and their son Herbert are enjoying a quiet evening playing chess by the fire when Sergeant-Major Morris, an old friend returning from India, arrives unexpectedly. Over whiskey, Morris reveals the existence of a monkey’s paw — a cursed talisman capable of granting three wishes to three men, but at a terrible cost, as its previous owner wished for death. Despite Morris’s warnings and his attempt to destroy the paw, Mr. White retrieves it, and under Herbert’s teasing provocation, he makes a careless wish for two hundred pounds. The paw twists violently in his hand, and an unsettling silence falls over the house, planting the first seed of dread.

The next morning, the family dismisses the incident as superstition, laughing off the paw’s power and leaving it forgotten on the sideboard. But that evening, a somber stranger from Herbert’s workplace arrives with devastating news: Herbert has been killed in a machinery accident, and the company offers exactly two hundred pounds in compensation — the precise amount Mr. White wished for. The horrifying coincidence shatters the family’s sense of reality; Mr. White collapses in shock, while Mrs. White is consumed by grief. The once-lighthearted home now hangs heavy with unspoken terror, as the supernatural force they dismissed begins to exact its price.

A week later, overwhelmed by inconsolable sorrow, Mrs. White demands her husband use the monkey’s paw to wish their son back to life. Terrified but powerless against her despair, Mr. White reluctantly makes the wish. As the night deepens, a slow, creeping knock begins at the front door — growing louder, more frantic — until it becomes violent pounding. Mrs. White, driven by desperate hope, rushes to open it, while Mr. White, realizing the horror of what awaits — a mangled, unnatural return — frantically searches for the paw. He finds it just as the final bolt is drawn and whispers his third and final wish. The knocking stops instantly. The house falls into an icy, suffocating silence, leaving the Whites alone with the unbearable weight of what they’ve unleashed and what they’ve lost.
